idiom_name: duck typing with respond_to?/respond_to_missing?; Object#extend singleton modules for per-object extension
implementation_notes: Ruby has no interface declarations, so the pattern's two halves collapse into duck typing: the client asks component.respond_to?(:next_word) (or calls the method and rescues NoMethodError) and the answer is computed from the object's singleton class and included modules, while the extension is supplied by extending that one object - component.extend(TextAccessor) includes a module into its singleton class at run time, adding methods no other instance of the class has. method_missing paired with a matching respond_to_missing? turns the lookup itself into the extension mechanism, and SimpleDelegator-style adapters remain the way to attach an extension that needs identity and state; this replaces the classic Extension hierarchy, at the cost that the capability set is invisible to static tools, so documentation and tests become the contract.
code_sketch:
module TextAccessor
  def words = @words ||= text.to_s.split
end

component.extend(TextAccessor) if component.respond_to?(:text) && !component.respond_to?(:words)
return unless component.respond_to?(:words)      # absence is a normal branch
component.words.each { |w| check(w) }
pitfalls: respond_to? can lie: a class using method_missing without respond_to_missing? reports false, so the probe and the call can disagree.
Singleton-class mutation is per-object and not thread-safe: two threads extending the same object concurrently can observe different method sets.
Frozen objects cannot be extended (FrozenError), and Ractor-shared objects reject per-object extension entirely.
Extending an object you do not own mutates behaviour for every later caller holding the same reference, invisibly.
